papers.title: Hole-doping induced ferromagnetism in 2D materials
papers.authors: Ruishen Meng, Lino da Costa Pereira, Jean-Pierre Locquet, Valeri Afanas’ev, Geoffrey Pourtois
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic materials are considered as promising candidates for the future generations of spintronic devices. Yet, 2D materials with intrinsic ferromagnetism are scarce. Hereby, high-throughput first-principles simulations are performed to screen 2D materials that present a non-magnetic to a ferromagnetic transition upon hole doping. A global evolutionary search is subsequently performed to identify alternative possible atomic structures of the eligible candidates, and 122 materials exhibiting a hole-doping induced ferromagnetism are identified. Their energetic and dynamic stability, as well as magnetic properties under hole doping are investigated systematically. Half of these 2D materials are metal halides, followed by chalcogenides, oxides, and nitrides, some of them having predicted Curie temperatures above 300 K. The exchange interactions responsible for the ferromagnetic order are also discussed. This work not only provides theoretical insights into hole-doped 2D ferromagnetic materials, but also enriches the family of 2D magnetic materials for possible spintronic applications.

papers.title: Antisite defect qubits in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides
papers.authors: Jeng-Yuan Tsai, Jinbo Pan, Hsin Lin, Arun Bansil, Qimin Yan
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Being atomically thin and amenable to external controls, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a new paradigm for the realization of patterned qubit fabrication and operation at room temperature for quantum information sciences applications. Here we show that the antisite defect in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can provide a controllable solid-state spin qubit system. Using high-throughput atomistic simulations, we identify several neutral antisite defects in TMDs that lie deep in the bulk band gap and host a paramagnetic triplet ground state. Our in-depth analysis reveals the presence of optical transitions and triplet-singlet intersystem crossing processes for fingerprinting these defect qubits. As an illustrative example, we discuss the initialization and readout principles of an antisite qubit in WS
                    2
                    , which is expected to be stable against interlayer interactions in a multilayer structure for qubit isolation and protection in future qubit-based devices. Our study opens a new pathway for creating scalable, room-temperature spin qubits in 2D TMDs.
papers.notes: Good reference for antisite defects in TMDs.

papers.title: Universal hydrogen-free synthesis and elemental doping of two-dimensional transition metal selenides
papers.authors: Ping Man, Lok Wing Wong, Ka Ho Leung, Zhiqiang Guan, Tianren Chen, Honglin Chen et al.
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal selenides (TMSs) feature notable bandgap flexibility, versatile doping characteristics, and practical manufacturability, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation electronics. However, their synthesis remains a critical bottleneck, as conventional chemical vapor deposition (CVD) routes require H2 assistance for selenization, raising safety, cost, and quality concerns and constraining elemental doping. Here we show a universal, H2-free CVD method that overcomes these limitations. Our approach produces a broad spectrum of 2D TMSs, including monolayer binaries, bilayer polytypes, alloys, and heterostructures, and is compatible with diverse substrates. Incorporating common metals (Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Cu) into the precursor enhances growth kinetics and enables precise doping. Al-doped WSe2 exhibits markedly lower resistance, with centimeter-scale films attaining a hole mobility of 28.36 cm2 V−1 s−1 and an on/off ratio of 3.56×106, comparable to exfoliated and H2-assisted monolayers. This work establishes a safe, scalable, and tunable synthesis strategy for high-performance 2D electronics. 2D transition metal selenides (TMSs) exhibit interesting (opto-)electronic properties, but their bottom-up synthesis usually requires H2 gas, leading to safety concerns and cost implications. Here, the authors report a universal H2-free chemical vapour deposition method to grow large-scale metal-doped 2D TMSs on various substrates.

papers.title: What Is the Role of a Magnetic Mo Antisite Defect on Carrier Relaxation and Spin Dynamics in 2-D MoS<sub>2</sub>?
papers.authors: Chengan Lei, Zhao Qian, Yandong Ma, Rajeev Ahuja
papers.abstract: Antisite defects significantly influence the dynamic properties of monolayer MoS 2, yet the carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in spin-polarized Mo antisite-defective MoS 2 remain unclear. Understanding these processes is crucial for advancing optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices. Here, we employ first-principles calculations and ab initio nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with spin–orbit coupling (SOC) to explore carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with a Mo antisite defect. This defect alters the material’s magnetic properties, leading to distinct relaxation behaviors: electron relaxation is slower than hole relaxation, and charge carriers in different spin channels exhibit varied dynamics. These differences arise from variations in electron–phonon coupling, SOC strength, and phonon mode activation. Our findings provide key insights into charge and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with magnetic defects and suggest strategies to enhance the performance of next-generation optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices.

papers.title: Antisite defect qubits in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides
papers.authors: Jeng-Yuan Tsai, Jinbo Pan, Hsin Lin, Arun Bansil, Qimin Yan
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Being atomically thin and amenable to external controls, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a new paradigm for the realization of patterned qubit fabrication and operation at room temperature for quantum information sciences applications. Here we show that the antisite defect in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can provide a controllable solid-state spin qubit system. Using high-throughput atomistic simulations, we identify several neutral antisite defects in TMDs that lie deep in the bulk band gap and host a paramagnetic triplet ground state. Our in-depth analysis reveals the presence of optical transitions and triplet-singlet intersystem crossing processes for fingerprinting these defect qubits. As an illustrative example, we discuss the initialization and readout principles of an antisite qubit in WS
                    2
                    , which is expected to be stable against interlayer interactions in a multilayer structure for qubit isolation and protection in future qubit-based devices. Our study opens a new pathway for creating scalable, room-temperature spin qubits in 2D TMDs.

news_articles.title: High-Throughput DFT Screening of 2D Transition Metal Carbonitrides for Solid-State Battery Solid Electrolyte Interphases
news_articles.affiliations: ¹ School of Advanced Materials Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU), Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea
news_articles.keywords: Solid-State Batteries, MXenes, DFT, High-Throughput Screening, VASP, LLZO
news_articles.abstract: The interface stability between garnet-type solid electrolytes (e.g., Li7La3Zr2O12, LLZO) and lithium metal anodes remains the primary bottleneck for next-generation solid-state batteries. We report a comprehensive high-throughput computational screening over 45 functionalized 2D transition metal carbonitrides (MXenes and MAB phases). By computing grand potential phase diagrams and interfacial reaction energies, we identify Ti3C2F2 and V2CTx as superior artificial SEI interlayers that effectively suppress lithium dendrite nucleation.
news_articles.content_html:
1. Background & Motivation

All-solid-state lithium metal batteries promise game-changing energy densities exceeding 500 Wh/kg. However, severe chemical side-reactions and dendrite propagation across the garnet electrolyte/lithium metal interface critically shorten cycle lifetime. In this study, we screen 2D transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) to design an ultra-thin, chemo-mechanically robust artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).

2. High-Throughput Computational Workflow

A Python-automated high-throughput DFT pipeline utilizing VASP and pymatgen screened 45 surface-terminated MXene compositions (M2X, M3X2, M4X3; M = Ti, V, Nb, Mo; Tx = O, F, OH, Cl). Li-ion diffusion pathways across the interfacial grain boundaries were evaluated using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method with 7 intermediate images.

ΔEinterface = Ebilayer - EMXene - ELLZO(001)

3. Interfacial Stability & Lithium Diffusion Barriers

Among all candidates, fluorinated titanium carbide Ti3C2F2 demonstrated an ideal balance of low Li-ion migration barrier (0.22 eV) and thermodynamic passivity against metallic lithium reduction. The computed grand-potential phase diagram indicates complete electrochemical stability from 0.0 V to 2.4 V vs Li/Li+.

4. Summary & Outlook

Our findings establish atomic-level design guidelines for stabilizing solid-state lithium battery interfaces, paving the way for targeted experimental synthesis in the upcoming quarter.

news_articles.keywords: High-Performance Computing, VASP 6.4, GPU Acceleration, Lab Facility, KIST Collaboration
news_articles.abstract: We are pleased to announce the successful installation and benchmarking of our new 128-core AMD EPYC 9554 computing node equipped with dual NVIDIA H100 GPUs, achieving a 4.2x speedup on hybrid functional calculations for 200+ atom supercells. In addition, our lab has signed a formal collaborative computing and experimental synthesis agreement with KIST Center for Computational Materials Science.
news_articles.content_html:
1. High-Performance Computing Cluster Expansion

To support high-throughput DFT simulations and hybrid functional calculations of large defect supercells, our research group has completed the deployment and commissioning of the SKKU-CMS-Node03 computing cluster. Specifications:

  • CPUs: Dual AMD EPYC 9554 processors (128 physical cores, 256 threads @ up to 3.75 GHz)
  • Memory: 512 GB DDR5-4800 ECC Registered RAM
  • Accelerators: 2x NVIDIA H100 PCIe (80 GB HBM3 each)
  • Storage: 8 TB NVMe PCIe Gen5 scratch storage for wavefunction and charge density I/O
  • Software Stack: VASP 6.4.2 compiled with OpenMPI 4.1.6, Intel oneMKL, and CUDA OpenACC GPU offloading

2. Benchmark Results on 2D Supercells

Benchmarking on a 216-atom 2D MoSi2N4 defect supercell with HSE06 hybrid functional demonstrated a 4.2× walltime reduction compared to our previous dual Xeon Gold nodes. Self-consistent electronic convergence was achieved within 38 minutes per k-point configuration.

3. Collaboration with KIST

Furthermore, under the new MoU with the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST), our group will gain access to shared supercomputing allocations on the KIST K-CREST infrastructure to perform ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations of molten salt synthesis.

news_articles.title: First-Principles Prediction of Two-Dimensional Ferroelectric Rashba Semiconductors in Janus Group-IV Chalcogenides
news_articles.authors: Vu Tien Lam¹*, Jaewon Kim¹, Jin-Woo Park²
news_articles.affiliations:
¹ School of Advanced Materials Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU), Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea
² Center for Computational Materials Science, Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST), Seoul 02792, Republic of Korea
news_articles.keywords: Janus Monolayers, Ferroelectricity, Rashba Effect, Spintronics, DFT
news_articles.abstract: Two-dimensional Janus monochalcogenides exhibit robust out-of-plane electric polarization and giant Rashba spin splitting. Here, through first-principles relativistic density functional theory calculations, we predict dynamic stability and room-temperature spontaneous electric polarization in Janus Ge2SeTe monolayers with strong spin-orbit coupling.
news_articles.content_html:
1. Introduction

Two-dimensional ferroelectrics with non-centrosymmetric structures provide an exceptional platform for nonvolatile spintronic memories. In this work, we investigate Janus group-IV monochalcogenide monolayers using hybrid DFT.

2. Methodology & Stabilities

Phonon dispersion curves calculated using density functional perturbation theory (DFPT) confirm kinetic stability across the full Brillouin zone without imaginary modes.

3. Rashba Spin Splitting

The broken inversion symmetry accompanied by vertical dipole gives rise to a giant Rashba parameter alpha_R = 1.82 eV·Å at the conduction band edge.

Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides host tightly bound excitons due to quantum confinement and reduced dielectric screening. We evaluate quasiparticle band gaps using single-shot G0W0 and partially self-consistent GW0.

news_articles.abstract: Electrical control of magnetism and valley states in two-dimensional semiconductors have been seeking for long time since they are essential for the application of low-power spintronic and valleytronic devices. Because non-magnetic Janus monolayer possesses inherent dipoles, which can provide a pathway to control them using external electric field. However, coupling these phenomena in Janus materials has been explored yet. Here we show that, using first-principles calculations, out-of-plane electric fields (Ez) and carrier doping synergistically drive itinerant Stoner ferromagnetism, which subsequently leads to anomalous valley Hall effect in monolayer MoSSe. An electric field of Ez ±1.0 V/Å triggers a giant Stark shift that pulls a conduction-band nearly free-electron state at the point across the Fermi level, inducing a metal-insulator transition. The elevated density of states at Fermi level satisfies the Stoner criterion, breaking combined parity-time symmetry and exhibiting polarity-selective orbital magnetization dominated by molybdenum and selenide states under positive and negative bias, respectively. This magnetic transition reverses the Berry curvature sign at the valley, deflecting carriers from both and valleys toward the same transverse edge. Introducing holes suppresses the delocalized free-electron states and strengthens exchange splitting, reopening the semiconducting gap with a valley splitting of 160 meV. Our findings highlight dual electrostatic and doping control as a versatile platform for electric spin-valleytronic devices. Γ -K K -K

Introduction

Reduced dimensionality and broken out-of-plane translational symmetry endow two-dimensional (2D) materials with unique electronic, valleytronic, and topological properties inaccessible in their bulk forms1,2. Among these systems, transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), with the general formula MX2, (where M is a transition metal and X is a chalcogen) have attracted substantial attention for nanoscale electronics and optoelectronics due to their direct bandgap transitions and pronounced spin–orbit coupling (SOC)3–5. Monolayer group-VI TMDs (such as , , etc.) host pairs of time-reversal-related, energetically degenerate valleys located at the and vertices of the first Brillouin zone6. In the monolayer limit, the absence of spatial inversion symmetry combined with strong SOC leads to robust spin–valley locking. This enables valley-selective optical excitation via circularly polarized light and allows control of carrier dynamics through both spin and valley degrees of freedom, positioning monolayer TMDs as an ideal platform for spintronics, valleytronics, and quantum information processing7,8. MoS2 WS2 K -K

Beyond conventional symmetric TMDs, replacing one of the two equivalent chalcogen layers of TMDs with a different chalcogen element was recently successfully demonstrated, referred to as Janus monolayer4,9. Typically, Janus MoSSe has been synthesized using chemical vapor deposition4,10,11. During the growth, one of S layers of MoS2 is replaced using hydrogen plasma and then, substitution of S with Se element follows using physical vapor deposition, eventually producing an asymmetric S–Mo–Se atomic configuration. The atomic structure of MoSSe implants an intrinsic dipole in out-of-plane direction. Thus, material properties of Janus MoSSe become highly controllable using an external electric field12,13. In particular, applying an external field to MoSSe gives rise to enhanced Rashba-type spin splitting and provides opportunities for controlling spin and valley degrees of freedom through external electric fields9,14–16.

Up to now, electrical control of electronic properties in 2D materials is highly attractive because it offers a reversible means of modifying the electronic structure without changing the chemical composition of the material. In atomically thin structures, a perpendicular electric field can redistribute charge, shift orbital energy states, and tune the band alignments14–18. For a polar Janus monolayer, however, the response is fundamentally different from that of a structurally symmetric sheet. The electric fields applied along opposite directions interact differently with the built-in dipole and with the chemically distinct chalcogen surfaces14,19,20. Field polarity can therefore influence not only the bandgap but also the orbital character of the states near the Fermi level21,22, opening the possibility of electrically driven changes in magnetic and valley behaviors. Despite considerable progress in understanding field-tunable Janus materials, the microscopic relationship among Stark-induced band reconstruction20,23, itinerant magnetism, and valley splitting in MoSSe remains to be fully clarified.

In this study, we investigate the effects of applied electric fields and hole doping on controlling the electronic, magnetic, and valley properties of monolayer MoSSe. The vertical external field at Ez = ±1.0 V/Å induces the Stark effect, resulting in the metal-insulator transition (MIT) with bandgap closure. In the conduction band, the spin energy states at each valley, and , are non-degenerated because of strengthened Rashba effects. When electronic states accumulate near the Fermi level, the increased density of states can favor spontaneous spin polarization according to the Stoner mechanism24–27. Interestingly, the carrier doping can promote Stoner-type ferromagnetism in low-dimensional materials25–27, suggesting that electrostatic and carrier-based control may act cooperatively rather than independently. We show that this interplay connects field-driven band reconstruction with orbital-selective magnetism and the lifting of valley degeneracy16,28, while hole doping further enhances the accessible magnetic and valley responses. These findings establish Janus MoSSe as a compelling platform in which charge, spin, and valley degrees of freedom can be controlled within the same material, with potential relevance to electrically reconfigurable spintronic and valleytronic devices. Results

Mechanical response to the electric field of Janus MoSSe

Figure 1(a) shows the optimized crystal structure of Janus MoSSe monolayer, while the inset of Fig. 1(b) highlights the asymmetric atomic configuration of the S–Mo–Se lattice relative atomic displacement with respect to central Mo atom layer. The top and bottom atomic layers are Se and S, respectively. To examine structural stability of MoSSe, we calculated phonon spectrum, showing no imaginary modes under representative electric fields (see Supplementary Fig. S1). Furthermore, the ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations retain the monolayer structure at 300 K over the simulated time interval for both the pristine and the biased configurations (see Supplementary Fig. S2 and Supplementary Note 1). These results verify that the Janus MoSSe monolayer is robust mechanically and stable thermally under the external electric field.

The dependence of geometry parameters of MoSSe monolayer on the vertical electric field (Ez) is systematically studied from Fig. 1(b) to Fig. 1(d). For instance, Fig. 1(b) highlights the total energy of Janus MoSSe monolayer as a function of applied electric field. At Ez = 2.0 V/Å, the energy difference between positive and negative field is observed to be 115 meV, which is invoked by the intrinsic dipole direction. Fig. 1(c) demonstrates the structural modulations in response to the applied field. Applying a positive field increases the distance between Mo–Se atoms while reducing the distance between Mo–S atoms. Overall, the monolayer thickness (S–Se distance, red line) increases in proportion to the external field. The atomic displacements of MoSSe are completely reversible under the positive fields, shown in Fig. 1(c). These structural variations are well consistent with previous results14. Interestingly, we found an anomalous change in the interatomic layer distance under the negative field direction. The distance of Mo–S (green line) increases in proportion to the field in Fig. 1(c) up to Ez = -1.2 V/Å, marked by a down head arrow, while that of Mo–Se (blue line) becomes shorter. However, above Ez = -1.2 V/Å, the atomic interlayer distance of Mo–S suddenly decreases, whereas that of Mo–Se increases, which is responsible for the overlap of electron wave functions. To benchmark the anomalous interlayer response against self-interaction errors inherent to local density approximations, atomic coordinates were re-relaxed using the Heyd-Scuseria Ernzerhof screened hybrid exchange-correlation functional29 (HSE06) yielding consistent structural parameters. as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. The HSE06 calculations yield nearly identical relative distance changes, confirming that this structural reversal is an intrinsic material response.

The induced polarization () and the macroscopic dipole moment () directly correlate with the structural evolution of the Mo-Se interatomic distance, as shown in Fig. 1(d). Under a positive bias, both and scale with the external field. However, they decrease at low field in the negative direction and then, a turn-up of them appears approximately at Ez = -1.2 V/Å. The minima of and observed on the negative-field direction occur because the intrinsic S–Mo–Se dipole actively counteracts to the external field, as it is explained in Fig. 1(c). The result implies that internal ionic displacements and electronic charge redistribution are highly attributed to the atomic displacement upon the external field and they strongly coupled together for the polarization. Electronic response and Stark effect of Janus MoSSe under an electric field

Next, we discuss electronic structure of Janus MoSSe under an external electric field. Figure 2(a) shows the electronic band structures of the pristine monolayer with (solid line) and without (dashed line) SOC. In both cases, the band edges occur at and valleys, indicating a direct bandgap at these high-symmetry points. The bandgap of MoSSe monolayer was calculated to be 1.559 eV and 1.445 eV without and with SOC, respectively. Electronic band structures were computed using the generalized gradient approximation parameterized by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof30 (GGA-PBE) alongside the HSE06 hybrid functional shown in Supplementary Figs. S5(a) and S5(b), respectively. Because the PBE functional accurately reproduces empirical monolayer dispersions reported in earlier studies9,11,31 while maintaining numerical tractability across dense field-dependent supercell grids, it was adopted for all subsequent finite-field and Berry-curvature evaluations.studies. To elucidate the underlying orbital hybridization that dictates these band edges, we present the orbital-resolved partial density of states (PDOS) in Fig. 2(b). The PDOS shows that both the valence band maximum (VBM) and conduction band minimum (CBM) are predominantly governed by Mo-4d orbitals, which are strongly hybridized with Se-4p and S-3p orbital states. To thoroughly compare the electronic structure, we calculated the field-dependent band structure using collinear, non-collinear, and fully SOC-inclusive formalisms as shown in Fig. 2(c). The collinear approach restricts electron spins to a single global quantization axis, whereas the non-collinear permits spin vectors to orient freely in three-dimensional space. The fully SOC-inclusive takes this a step further by coupling these unconstrained spin degrees of freedom directly to the crystal lattice, providing the rigorous physical framework necessary to capture relativistic effects like spin-valley locking32. Despite these fundamentally different treatments of spin density, all three methods yield a remarkable consistency, i.e., the sudden bandgap closing near the critical field strengths of Ez = ±1.0 V/Å because of the giant Stark effect. The metal-insulator transitions (MIT) using the external electric field were observed from various layered materials including MoSe2, GaAs, and GaSe33–35. Furthermore, employing such a high field (up to ±2.0 V/Å) is experimentally feasible through the integration of high- gate dielectrics, as corroborated by finite-element electrostatic simulations using COMSOL (see Supplementary Note 3 and Fig. S6). κ

Figure 2(d) and 2(e) present electronic band structure of MoSSe under various electric fields in both positive and negative directions, respectively. At Ez = ±0.4 V/Å, MoSSe monolayer is still a semiconductor with bandgap of approximately 1.44 eV. However, the bandgap starts decreasing sharply above Ez = ±0.8 V/Å, which accompanies the entering of first nearly free-electron (NFE) states from the conduction band into the bandgap, marked by red dotted curves. Therefore, the bandgap reduces to 1.011 eV at Ez = ±0.8 V/Å and decreases sharply at stronger field strength. Then, the bandgap completely closes above Ez = ±1.0 V/Å, driving the semiconducting to fully metallic state of MoSSe. More progressive bandgap closing at various field ranges (0 to ±2.0 V/Å) is presented in Supplementary Figs. S7-S10. It should be noted that, from the conduction, the highly delocalized NFE states only at G valley is responsive to the external field36. Compared to the strongly localized valence band maximum, the NFE states are more sensitive to an external field, consistent with previous first-principles studies37,38. Furthermore, as shown in Figs. 2(d) and 2(e) together with Supplementary Figs. S7 and S8, at Ez = ±1.0 V/Å, NFE states split because of SOC and the lower state of NFE ones crosses the Fermi level. In the field range between Ez = ±1.2 and ±1.4 V/Å, these two NFE states overlap because the field-induced Stark shift overcomes their initial SOC-induced energy splitting. Similar interplay between the Stark effect and SOC, leading to substantial band-energy reconstruction, has been reported in few-layer black arsenic39. Interestingly, above Ez = ±1.6 V/Å, however, these two NFE states split again owing to the enhanced Rashba-type SOC under the strong inversion-symmetry-breaking electric field. Simultaneously, the strong Stark response of the spatially delocalized NFE states has them cross over the bandgap. The origin of the overlap and movement of NFE states are also observed in the band structure calculated without SOC (see Supplementary Figs. S9 and S10).

To elucidate the origin of the field-induced Stark effect, we present a diagram detailing the physical mechanism governing the bandgap reduction in Janus MoSSe monolayer in Fig. 2(f). The intrinsic bandgap Eg at zero field is dictated by the orbital hybridization between the transition metal and the chalcogen atoms. The conduction band edge is primarily composed of Mo- orbitals hybridized with out-of-plane S/Se- orbitals, whereas the valence band is dominated by in-plane Mo- orbitals hybridized with S/Se- states. When an external field is applied, it introduces an electrostatic potential gradient across the finite thickness of the monolayer, triggering a pronounced Stark shift. This potential gradient lowers the energy of the conduction band minimum states, downshifting them toward the Fermi level, while simultaneously pushing the valence band maximum ones upward slightly. Hole doping induces Valley non-degeneracy and Stoner magnetism in Janus MoSSe

Beyond purely field-driven metallization, carrier doping is widely utilized to engineer the magnetic and topological phases of 2D materials. The top of the valence band is dominated by strongly localized Mo- orbitals with a large effective mass and features nearly degenerate extrema at , , and points. Hole doping shifts the Fermi level deeper into these localized valence states, causing a sharp and non-linear rise in the Fermi-level density of states . The increased allows the system to readily satisfy the Stoner criterion even at moderate electric field magnitudes. In the absence of an external electric field, the valley degeneracy remains unchanged across all doping concentrations (Fig. S18(a)-(c)). Therefore, an external electric field must be applied synergistically with the hole doping to achieve the desired valley degeneracy lifting via spin-state splitting. 4d K -K Γ DEF DEF

Discussion

We propose the polar Janus MoSSe monolayer as a highly adaptable platform for integrated electromechanical and spin-valleytronic applications. While the pristine lattice maintains stable dynamical properties and a direct bandgap of 1.445 eV, applying a vertical electric field forces a severe electronic reconstruction. The combination of intrinsic structural inversion asymmetry and a massive Stark effect drives a nonlinear lattice distortion, culminating in a metal-insulator transition (MIT) at critical field strengths of ±1.0 V/Å. Once driven into this metallic phase, the reconfigured electronic structure satisfies the Stoner criterion, triggering spontaneous itinerant ferromagnetism. Mulliken population analyses confirm that this emergent magnetic state is spatially segregated and highly tunable, with magnetization localized primarily on the Mo atoms under positive bias and the Se atoms under negative bias.

Furthermore, magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) evaluations confirm that this field-induced ferromagnetic ground state is stabilized by a robust perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, accompanied by a highly tunable in-plane directional preference (see Supplementary Note 6 and Figs. S32–S33). To further expand this functionality, we introduced carrier doping as a synergistic tuning mechanism. Hole doping effectively suppresses the delocalized nearly free-electron (NFE) states and relocalized active charge carriers, drastically amplifying the valley splitting up to 160 meV between the and valleys. Consequently, the simultaneous modulation of electrostatic fields and carrier concentration provides a viable, purely electrical method for manipulating Stoner magnetism and controlling robust valley Hall transport in two-dimensional technologies. Further work will be necessary to establish the experimental feasibility and thermal stability of the device for practical, nonvolatile spin-valleytronic memory and logic applications. K -K

Calculation details

First-principles density functional theory (DFT) simulations were performed using the plane-wave pseudopotential codes Cambridge Serial Total Energy Package (CASTEP)59 and Quantum ESPRESSO (QE)60. Electronic exchange and correlation were described via the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)30, which reliably captures structural and electronic trends across periodic 2D systems at tractable computational cost. To benchmark the field-driven bond-length anomalies and pristine band edges, additional hybrid-functional calculations were conducted using the Heyd–Scuseria–Ernzerhof (HSE06) hybrid functional29. Plane-wave basis functions were expanded up to a kinetic energy cutoff of 1350 eV. Structural relaxations were iterated until energy variations and atomic Hellmann–Feynman forces fell below 10-6 eV, and 10-4 eV/Å, respectively. Reciprocal-space integration across the 2D Brillouin zone (BZ) employed a -centered 12 × 12 × 1 Monkhorst–Pack k-point mesh61, whereas single-point magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) evaluations utilized a denser 21 × 21 × 1 mesh. An 18 Å vacuum layer was placed along the z direction to minimize interactions between periodically repeated monolayers. Spin-orbit coupling was also taken into account when evaluating the spin-valley interaction, band splitting and determining the MAE. We have used the WANNIER90 code60,62,63 (implemented in QE) to compute the Berry curvature and carried out postdata processing. Carrier doping was modeled by removing electrons out of the system, and a uniform background charge is adopted to maintain charge neutrality. The structural visualizations were rendered using VESTA software64. To quantitatively assess the spatial redistribution of charge carriers and the localization behavior of the nearly free electron (NFE) states, we computed the electron localization function (ELF)65. In the case of strong localization, the value is nearly unity (e.g., within the Mo-d or Se-p orbitals), whereas the value of near 0.5 characterizes highly delocalized states.
